Match: match_0204
Innings: 1
Fields:
- inn1.total_runs
- inn1.total_wickets

Commentary:
At Willow Bank Ground in Easthaven, Seabrook won the toss and chose to bat in a final that turned into something far tighter and stranger than the first-innings target would later suggest, because Moorland spent most of the day holding control, losing it briefly, then having to win it back under real pressure. Seabrook were under stress almost immediately when Ravi Stone edged Arjun Reed to Nathan Grant before the innings had properly formed, and that first wicket mattered because it pushed the batting side into repair mode from the opening over. Miles Harper became the long thread of the innings, but this was not the kind of anchoring hand that lets a side dictate the game; it was survival, dead-bat resistance, and small scraps of movement while partners came and went. Julian Cross stayed with him for a while but was run out before the score had reached anything safe, and even that early stand leaned heavily on extras, which became one of the themes of the innings. Tristan Vale, the captain, then produced Seabrook’s first real counterpunch, striking three boundaries in a brisk sixteen, and for a moment the innings looked as though it might escape the squeeze. Arjun Reed cut that off, Lucas Grant taking the catch, and Ryan Cole then made the next phase even more damaging by removing Evan Hart, Logan Hart, and Simon Frost in a middle-order burst that reduced Seabrook to sixty-three for six. That was the section where Moorland should have buried the innings completely. Nathan Shaw was drying one end with almost no release, Ryan was finding wickets, and Arjun’s early impact had already unsettled the card. Seabrook, though, kept finding just enough stubborn resistance to make Moorland work longer than they wanted. Daniel Cross made only four from thirty-eight balls, but he stayed beside Miles Harper long enough to add nineteen. Tyler Quinn then gave the innings its most useful lower-middle pulse, ten from seventeen, and with Miles he helped drag the total beyond three figures. Arjun returned to bowl Tyler, and Nathan Shaw finally ended Miles Harper’s long stay at one hundred and four, leaving Seabrook nine down with the innings still looking thin. The last pair of Marcus Flynn and Liam Brooks changed the tone slightly. It was not fluent, and it was not enough to make the total genuinely strong, but their fifteen-run stand forced Moorland into the fortieth over and lifted Seabrook to one hundred and nineteen all out. Marcus made eleven before Caleb Turner finished the innings, while Liam Brooks stayed not out after a long defensive stay. The card told a clear story: Seabrook’s batters made only ninety-five runs, their total was heavily supported by twenty-four extras, and no batter went beyond Miles Harper’s thirty. Moorland’s bowling was strong in structure even if not perfectly clean. Arjun Reed struck early, returned later, and finished with three wickets. Ryan Cole’s three wickets broke the middle. Nathan Shaw’s ten overs for fifteen were the most suffocating spell in the innings. Caleb Turner closed the lower order, while Luke Parker’s quiet overs helped keep Seabrook from finding a proper release point. Chasing one hundred and twenty, Moorland should have had a controlled path, and for a few overs they looked as though they might make the final simple. Ethan Vale struck three early boundaries before Daniel Cross held a return catch, and Lucas Grant then counterattacked with eighteen from fourteen, including a six, to make the target feel small. But Daniel Cross changed the match completely. He removed Lucas, trapped Noah Grant first ball, then later dismissed Owen Barrett, and by the time Liam Brooks also removed Connor Hayes, Moorland were fifty-eight for five. A chase that had looked close to routine had become a final full of noise. Caleb Turner and Dylan Price slowed it down with the most important repair of the chase, adding thirty-one. Caleb made eighteen from forty-two and gave Dylan the time he needed, while Dylan stayed calm enough to let the target shrink rather than force a finish that was not yet there. Marcus Flynn broke that stand at eighty-nine, and Seabrook struck again almost immediately. Tyler Quinn bowled Luke Parker, then trapped Nathan Shaw lbw, and suddenly Moorland were ninety for eight with thirty still required. That was the true tension point of the final. Seabrook had Daniel Cross’s four-wicket spell behind them, Tyler Quinn had just cracked the lower order, and one more wicket would have exposed Ryan Cole with the target still far enough away to create panic. Dylan Price was still there, and that mattered. His unbeaten twenty-five from fifty-two was not elegant, but it was the innings that refused to let the chase completely collapse. Arjun Reed then walked in and gave the match its finishing logic. He had already taken three wickets, yet his unbeaten eighteen from thirteen balls became just as important because it gave Dylan a partner who could do more than survive. Arjun struck one boundary, cleared the rope once, and shifted the pressure back toward Seabrook at the only moment when they truly looked capable of stealing the final. The last stand was worth thirty with no extras, which is crucial because this was not a finish gifted by wides or no-balls; it was won by two batters under pressure. Dylan controlled one end, Arjun supplied the decisive strokes, and Moorland reached one hundred and twenty for eight in the thirty-first over. The match was therefore not a clean chase of a small target; it was a low-scoring final full of pressure transfers. Seabrook’s innings was held together by Miles Harper’s occupation, Tyler Quinn’s short resistance, and the late Marcus-Liam stand, while Moorland’s reply nearly broke under Daniel Cross and Tyler Quinn before Dylan Price and Arjun Reed rescued it. Arjun Reed was the correct Player of the Match because his performance touched both decisive halves: he damaged Seabrook’s innings with the ball, then returned at ninety for eight to help finish the chase. Moorland won by two wickets and became winners, but they did it the hard way, through bowling control, a tense lower-order recovery, and one all-round contribution that mattered exactly when the final was most alive.

Commentary:
Good morning from Westbrook College Ground in Fairhaven, where this second semi-final of the match became a match of immediate control, short resistance, and one chase handled with the calm of a side that knew it had already done the hard work. Ridgeway won the toss, chose to field, and that decision began to look correct almost before Seacliff had found a rhythm, because Owen Vale struck in the opening over and made the top order feel as if it had walked into a match already moving too quickly for it. Ravi Stone went first, bowled after only a tiny start, and Isaac Hart followed before the innings had found any kind of base. Miles Harper tried to stay, Tyler Brooks tried to absorb, but the scoreboard kept resetting after every small movement. Nathan Reed then added to the damage by removing Miles Harper, and Owen Vale’s lbw against Tyler Brooks meant Seacliff were already four down with barely anything on the board. Evan Cole briefly suggested a release when he found the rope, but that was no more than a flicker. Nathan Reed removed Liam Porter, Owen Vale came back for Cole Bennett, and then Nathan closed off Evan Cole as well, leaving Seacliff twenty for seven before the innings had even reached the point where a normal batting side begins thinking about consolidation. That was the defining section of the semi-final. It was not simply that wickets fell; it was the way they fell too close together for Seacliff to form any centre of gravity. The extras column did some of the moving, small wides and stray deliveries keeping the total from freezing completely, but the bat itself gave almost no resistance through the first half. The one passage that forced Ridgeway to work again came from Lucas Grant and Jordan Hayes. Their stand of twenty-two was modest in ordinary terms, but in the context of this innings it was the only partnership that looked like actual batting rather than emergency survival. Lucas was the more assertive hand, finding two boundaries and giving Seacliff their first proper shape, while Jordan Hayes stayed long enough to let the stand breathe. Connor Hale broke that partnership by bowling Jordan, and Luke Parker’s short spell around that phase carried real weight because two overs, two maidens and one wicket left no escape route at the other end. When Lucas was trapped by Luke, Seacliff were nine down and still short of anything that could worry Ridgeway. Aiden Ross gave the last piece of resistance, making ten, and with Gavin Moore he dragged the total to fifty-eight before Caleb Turner ended the innings. Seacliff’s total was low, but the internal structure made it look even weaker: only forty-six came from the bat, only Lucas and Aiden reached double figures, and seven wickets had fallen before the eighth-wicket stand briefly brought a little order. Ridgeway’s bowling card was therefore best read as a connected demolition. Owen Vale’s four wickets set the emotional direction of the match. Nathan Reed’s three wickets ensured there was no middle-order recovery. Luke Parker froze the scoring completely. Connor Hale and Caleb Turner made sure the tail could not turn irritation into a defendable total. Chasing fifty-nine in a semi-final can still become awkward if the first wicket starts a panic, and Seacliff did give themselves one small opening. Adrian Cole struck a boundary and then edged Cole Bennett through to Miles Harper, so Ridgeway were one down early enough for the fielding side to shout, gather around the bat, and imagine a messy finish. Ethan Blake and Mason Reed did not let that happen. Ethan played the steadier hand, not rushing the chase, punishing width when it arrived, and keeping the scoreboard moving with just enough authority to prevent pressure from forming. Mason Reed gave him the perfect small-target support: calm, clean, and unhurried, with two boundaries and no need to chase spectacle. Their unbeaten stand of fifty-five turned the reply from a potential trap into a controlled passage. Seacliff also hurt themselves with extras, because thirteen free runs in a defence of fifty-eight is too much to survive, and Liam Porter’s spell in particular kept releasing pressure whenever the fielding side needed dots. Cole Bennett’s early wicket remained the only real moment of resistance. Aiden Ross could not create a second breakthrough, and once Ethan and Mason settled, the chase became less a contest than a formality being handled professionally. Ridgeway reached sixty for one in the ninth over, winning by nine wickets and qualifying, and the result reflected the shape of the match exactly. Seacliff had one stand through Lucas Grant and Jordan Hayes, one late hand from Aiden Ross, and a single early wicket in the reply. Ridgeway had the real structure: Owen Vale breaking the top order, Nathan Reed deepening the collapse, Luke Parker choking the middle, the support bowlers closing the innings, and then Ethan Blake with Mason Reed finishing the chase without drama. Owen Vale was the right Player of the Match because his spell did not merely collect wickets; it decided the semi-final’s direction before Seacliff had time to build. By the time Ridgeway crossed the line, match looked not like a late achievement but like the natural conclusion of a match they had controlled from the first over.
